segments.text: Welcome back.
Day sixteen.
You've just brought something to mind.
You don't need to tell me what it is.
Keep it nearby.
We'll come back to it.
Sooner or later, something heavy lands.
A bad day at work.
An argument.
News you didn't want.
And an old thought arrives right on time.
"This is exactly when I'd have had one."
Remember what you saw in the prep week.
Stress and the gap feel alike, and they stack.
Nicotine closed the gap.
The stress, the real thing, was still sitting there afterwards.
The email.
The bill.
The argument.
So you're not facing hard days with something missing.
You're facing them without the extra layer on top.
Studies of people who stopped smoking found that, once withdrawal settled, they were on average less anxious and less stressed than people who kept smoking.
What's left is the feeling itself.
And a feeling doesn't have to be fixed, or fought, or got rid of.
It can be made room for.
Let's do that now, with the thing you brought to mind.
Take a breath, in a way that feels comfortable for you.
If focusing on your breath doesn't feel good, just breathe normally and notice your feet on the floor instead.
Let the thing come closer.
Not all the way.
Just enough to feel it.
Find where it lands in your body.
A weight in your chest.
A knot in your stomach.
Tight shoulders.
Now, instead of bracing against it, see if you can soften around it.
As if you were making the space a little bigger, so it has room to sit.
You're not trying to make it leave.
You're letting it be here, and breathing anyway.
Notice that you can hold this and still be all right.
It's heavy.
And you're holding it.
Now let it move back to where it was.
That's sixty seconds.
Feel the feeling first, then decide what to do about the problem.
In the prep week you made two plans for stress.
In a moment they'll be on your screen, with a check-in to see where the feeling is now.
And if what you're carrying is more than a bad day, please don't carry it alone.
If low mood lasts more than about two weeks, or gets in the way of daily life, please talk to your doctor.
And if you ever feel you can't cope or keep yourself safe, get help straight away.
There are numbers for where you live in the app.
Big feelings pass too.
You can make room for them.
I'll see you in a few days.
